Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Use an LLM API to get next-token probabilities for a prompt. Write that always picks the highest-probability token to build a sentence word by word. Got it? Skip to Part 5 .
A large language model (LLM) does something remarkably simple: Given some text, it predicts probabilities for the next token .

fragments.text: For example, given , an LLM might output: Token Probability mat 0.35 floor 0.20 roof 0.15 bed 0.10 table 0.08
The simplest strategy: always pick the most probable token . This is called greedy decoding .

slide_text: Part 7: The Problem with Greedy Choices

Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Instead of keeping just one candidate sentence, keep the top [math] candidates at each step, expanding each one with all possible next tokens, then keeping only the best [math] overall. Write . Got it? Skip to the end .
Consider this scenario. The LLM gives these probabilities: Token A (0.6) Token B (0.4) Then next: A X (0.3) B Y (0.9) Total: [math] [math]

fragments.text: Greedy picks A first (0.6 0.4). But the path through B is twice as good overall (0.36 vs 0.18)!
The locally best choice isn t always the globally best path. How do we fix this without trying every possible sequence (which grows exponentially)?

slide_text: The idea: instead of keeping one candidate at each step, keep the top [math] best candidates.

fragments.text: At each step: Take your [math] current candidates. For each candidate, try all possible next tokens. Score every extension: candidate s score [math] new token s probability. Keep only the top [math] overall.

It s like exploring a tree, but instead of one path (greedy) or all paths (exhaustive), you keep [math] beams of light shining through the most promising branches. This is called beam search , and [math] is the beam width .

Step 2: expand both candidates, score all extensions, keep top 2 again. The beam explores two promising paths in parallel!
